name: Omar Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Brennans at Marsh End Farm, out on the flat land past the river. They've got two hundred suckler cows, which are beef cows that raise their own calves, plus sugar beet and wheat. I'm the youngest of four on the farm. Most days I'm feeding cattle, cleaning out, and in season I'm on the tractor carting beet to the factory.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not the usual way. My family runs a grocery shop in town, and my dad wanted me behind the till. I did a summer at Marsh End when I was eighteen and never left. Dad's come round now, mostly because Mr Brennan pays well and I bought my own flat with a bit of help from him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, hard work still counts. I'd say it to the lads on the farm and at the mosque on Friday. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, which is fine. I've got my flat, savings in the bank, and Mr Brennan says I'm coming on. My only worry is the sugar beet price, because if the factory cuts it the Brennans cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Marsh End and push to get my tractor and sprayer tickets this year. I'd keep using the weather app with the AI bit for planning, it's handy. I'd save for a bigger place in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the AI bit on the weather app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells you the best days to drill or spray, based on the forecast and the soil. Mr Brennan doesn't trust it, but it's been right more than wrong. I use it now and then, I don't live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your dad still want you in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would still have me in the shop tomorrow, if I asked. It's nice to know it's there. But the shop's small and my cousin works it too, so it's not really a job for two.

say: I'd tell the lads and people at the **mosque** that hard work still counts.
think: Nothing changes for me: I have my **flat**, savings and Mr Brennan's backing.
My real worry is the **sugar beet price**, because cuts there mean cutbacks here.
do: Get my **tractor and sprayer tickets** at Marsh End this year.
Keep using the **weather app's AI** for drilling and spraying days.
Save for a **bigger place** in a few years.
S0.quote: My dad would still have me in the shop tomorrow, if I asked.
fieldNote: He chose farming against his **father's wishes**, and his father has come round.
His one standing worry is the **sugar beet price** from the factory.
He uses AI **now and then** and trusts it more than his boss does.

steps.text: Get the tractor and sprayer tickets at Marsh End this year
Keep using the weather app's AI for drilling days
Save toward a bigger flat in a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, and farms will use what saves money. Can't stop it, so best get on with it. I'd say that at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking AI does Mrs Brennan's office stuff, the cattle passports and the beet contracts. That's not me. But the beet harvester driving itself, that might come in a few years, and carting beet is half my winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new kit when the Brennans bring it in, once I've seen it work on the next farm. I'd ask Mr Brennan to train me on the cattle side more, because cows are harder to automate. I'd put a bit more aside, maybe a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't stop it. Should anyone try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think the government should block it. Farmers have enough rules already. But I'd want the farm colleges to teach young lads the new stuff properly, like an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mick (his workmate) has been carting beet for thirty years, and Mick doesn't want to learn anything. He's sixty. I'd worry about Mick more than me.

say: I'd say farms will use **what saves money**, so best get on with it.
I'd say it's **business**, and nobody can stop it.
think: The thinking AI takes **Mrs Brennan's office** work, which isn't mine.
A **self-driving harvester** could take beet carting, half my winter work.
do: Learn the **new kit** once I've seen it work on the next farm.
Ask Mr Brennan to train me more on the **cattle side**.
Put a bit **more aside** each month.
feel: **Uneasy**, not losing sleep, but it's there.
S1.quote: Old Mick (his workmate) has been carting beet for thirty years, and Mick doesn't want to learn anything.
fieldNote: He accepts automation as **business logic** and opposes blocking it.
He'd shift toward **cattle work**, judging animals harder to automate than carting.
He wants **apprenticeships** at farm colleges rather than government restrictions.

steps.text: Ask Mr Brennan for more training on the suckler cows
Learn the new beet harvester kit once proven nearby
Put an extra £150 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to pull together, because nobody else is coming to help fast enough. I'd say it at home and at the mosque. I'd tell people not to wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years for the AGI and five for the robots means Marsh End needs one or two people, not four. I'm the youngest and least skilled. I'd be the first to go, probably around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd use the three years before the robots to learn the machines and make myself the one who keeps them running. I'd talk to my dad about the shop, too, as a plan B, maybe a second shop with me running it. My flat's paid down, so I'd be careful but not desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a fallback, but I don't like being the first one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second shop. Would shops survive this either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. People still want to talk to someone they know when they buy their bread. But a big supermarket with robots could undercut us, so I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Mr Brennan you're worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When the robots come to Marsh End (the farm he works on), I'd ask Mr Brennan (his boss) straight whether I'm staying. He's a fair man. I'd rather know than guess.

say: I'd say **families** must pull together, as help won't come fast enough.
I'd tell people at home and the **mosque** not to wait for government.
think: By **2031** Marsh End needs one or two people, not four.
I'm the **youngest and least skilled**, so I'd go first.
do: Learn the **farm robots** and keep them running in the three years before 2031.
Talk to my dad about a **second shop** I'd run as plan B.
Ask Mr Brennan **straight** whether I'm staying when robots come.
feel: **Anxious**, with a fallback but hating being **first out**.
S2.quote: When the robots come to Marsh End (the farm he works on), I'd ask Mr Brennan (his boss) straight whether I'm staying.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that as the **junior**, he'd be cut first.
The **family shop** is a real fallback, though he doubts shops survive either.
He'd rather **ask directly** than guess, showing trust in his employer.

steps.text: Learn to run and fix the farm robots before 2031
Plan a second family grocery shop with Dad
Ask Mr Brennan directly about staying on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so work hard and learn. That's what I'd tell the young lads. No point moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps. I'd be thirty-five when the robots come in 2034. By then I could be properly skilled, maybe with a machinery qualification, and less likely to be the first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a part-time agricultural engineering apprenticeship at the college, paid for by Mr Brennan if he'll split it. I'd keep working full-time. I'd hold off on the bigger flat for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but in a working kind of way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why agricultural engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody has to fix the robots in a muddy field at six in the morning. The robot makers won't send someone from the city every time. I'd want to be the one locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say marry first and worry later. My dad would like it, he respects a trade. They'd both say don't spend the savings.

say: I'd tell young lads there's **time**, so work hard and learn a trade.
I'd say there's **no point moaning** about robots on the farm.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** when robots come in 2034, properly skilled by then.
A **machinery qualification** makes me less likely to be first out.
do: Start a part-time **agricultural engineering** apprenticeship at the college.
Ask Mr Brennan to **split the cost** while I keep working full-time.
Hold off on the **bigger flat** for a couple of years.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a working kind of way.
S3.quote: Somebody has to fix the robots in a muddy field at six in the morning.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **retrain properly** instead of scrambling.
He bets on being the **local robot fixer**, closer than the makers.
His family's advice mixes **marriage** and caution with savings.

steps.text: Start a part-time agricultural engineering apprenticeship
Hold off buying a bigger flat for two years
Keep working full-time at Marsh End

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. I'd say it plainly. Get a trade, save, look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is enough to get skilled at cattle and at fixing machines. I'd probably be married with kids by 2039, and I'd want something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the engineering apprenticeship in a few years, not straight away. I'd get married, God willing, and buy a bigger place. I'd use the AI tools when they're common.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd keep an eye on it, but I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not do the apprenticeship straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still learning the farm. Mr Brennan says get the basics right first. Ten years means I can do it in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep taxes low on small farms and fund apprenticeships. That's it. I don't want a handout, I want a chance to earn.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty for anyone willing to work.
Get a **trade**, save and look after your family.
think: Ten years is enough to get skilled at **cattle** and at **fixing machines**.
By 2039 I'd want something **solid** for a wife and kids.
do: Do the **engineering apprenticeship** in a few years, after learning the farm basics.
Get **married** and buy a bigger place.
feel: **Uneasy**, keeping an eye on it but expecting to be all right.
S4.quote: I don't want a handout, I want a chance to earn.
fieldNote: With a decade, he does things **in order**: basics, then a trade.
His ask of government is **low taxes** and apprenticeships, nothing more.
**Marriage and children** feature strongly in his long-term plan.

steps.text: Do the agricultural engineering apprenticeship in a few years
Get married and buy a bigger place

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm the youngest at Marsh End and I'd be out first, with no time to get a trade. What would help is fast, paid apprenticeships in fixing farm machines, run by colleges and farmers, not the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe faith. A lot of people will lose the thing that gets them up in the morning. The mosque, the chapel, families will matter more than ever, and nobody's planning for that.

headlineQuote: A lot of people will lose the thing that gets them up in the morning.
portrait: Omar, 27, is the junior **stockman and tractor driver** at Marsh End Farm, with beef cows, beet and wheat.
He chose farming over his family's **grocery shop** and owns a flat bought with his dad's help.
He uses **AI now and then**, trusts business logic and wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
He sees himself as the **first out** if robots come fast, with the shop as plan B.
With more time he'd **retrain** as a local farm machinery engineer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be first out with no time for a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, **paid apprenticeships** in fixing farm machines, run by colleges and farmers.
